qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture six. Consistency and consensus. This is what it costs to make many machines agree.
Many machines, called nodes, talk over a network. A node can crash.
A node can crash.
A message can get lost, and that node never hears.
A message can get lost.
A reply can arrive very late.
A reply can arrive late.
Or the network can split in two.
The network can split in two.
Two copies hold the tickets left for the show, forty each.
Two copies hold the tickets left.
Then the link between them is cut.
The link between them is cut.
A sale of five tickets reaches only node A, which now says thirty-five.
A sale reaches only one copy.
Now node B is asked to read.
Node B is asked to read.
If it refuses, the answer is never wrong, but it is not available.
Refuse: right, but not available.
If it answers forty, it is available, but stale.
Answer: available, but stale.
Asha has one hundred pounds, and Ben has fifty. Moving thirty pounds is two writes.
Moving £30 is two writes.
A crash hits after the debit, before the credit.
A crash hits after the debit.
Now thirty pounds has vanished. The total is one hundred and twenty.
£30 has vanished.
Inside one transaction, the debit is undone.
One transaction undoes the debit.
It is all or nothing, so the total stays one hundred and fifty.
All or nothing: the total stays £150.
Two shoppers each pay thirty pounds from a balance of one hundred.
Two shoppers pay £30.
Both read one hundred before either writes.
Both read £100 first.
Both write seventy, so one payment is lost.
Both write £70: one is lost.
One at a time gives the right answer, forty.
One at a time gives £40.
Together these make acid. Atomic, consistent, isolated and durable.
ACID: atomic, consistent, isolated, durable.
A write of thirty-five lands on one copy.
The write lands on one copy.
The others hear later, one hop at a time.
The others hear later.
A read now, at the third copy, still returns forty. It is stale.
A read now can be stale.
Soon every copy agrees. That is eventual consistency.
Soon every copy agrees.
The goal is that many copies act like one.
Many copies should act like one.
Each bar is one operation, spread over time. Client C is writing the value one.
Each bar is one operation in time.
One flip moment, inside the write, explains every read.
One flip explains every read.
Now client B reads zero, after client A read one.
Now B reads 0 after A read 1.
No flip moment fits. This history is not linearizable.
No flip fits: not linearizable.
Two sites, London and Leeds, both sell seat fourteen C.
Two sites sell seat 14C.
Each books its own customer, Mia and Omar, without asking.
Each books its own customer.
Neither knew about the other, so the seat is sold twice.
Neither knew: sold twice.
So Leeds must ask London first, and Omar is refused.
So Leeds must ask London first.
Asking costs sixty-two milliseconds, not two, as the messages take thirty each way.
Asking costs 62 ms, not 2 ms.
One purchase touches several databases, and they must all agree.
Several databases must agree.
A coordinator just sends commit to all of them.
It just sends commit to all.
One commits, one hits a conflict, and one never hears.
One conflicts, one never hears.
Now the databases disagree about the purchase.
Now the databases disagree.
Two-phase commit has two phases. First, ask every database to vote.
First, ask every database.
Each one votes, and holds its locks while it waits.
Each votes, and holds its locks.
Payments votes no, and any no means abort for all.
Any no means abort for all.
All three abort and unlock.
All three abort and unlock.
If all had voted yes, all would commit.
If all vote yes, all commit.
When the network is cut, refuse to answer, or answer with stale data.
Act like one copy, so that no read goes back in time.
Two-phase commit means all say yes, or everything aborts.
